- If sentiment history shows a recent negative signal (e.g., -1.00), model should reduce forecast slope or shift downward to avoid over-optimism.  
- When model forecasts show a steady upward trend with no recent dip, true outcomes often exhibit sharp downward corrections — especially after a spike — suggesting model overestimates near-term upside.  
- If true outcomes show a strong downward trend (e.g., 50s–60s drop) and model remains flat or rising, model is underestimating downside risk — adjust downward by 5–10% of forecast range.  
- Model tends to overcorrect after a spike — if forecast rises sharply after a dip, true outcome often follows a “rebound” or “reversion” to prior mean — reduce forecast slope after spike.  
- If sentiment is neutral or positive (0.00) and model is rising steadily, true outcome often shows a “mean reversion” or “pullback” — reduce forecast by 2–5% for next period.  
- Model often fails to account for sentiment-driven volatility — if sentiment is negative, true outcome may dip more than model predicts — apply a “sentiment penalty” to forecast (e.g., subtract 1–3% of forecast value).  
- For 30-day horizon, model tends to overestimate recovery — true outcome often shows a “slowdown” or “reversal” after initial rise — adjust forecast downward by 3–7% for next 10–15 days.
